`git rebase --onto` lets you choose exactly which commits get moved and where they end up. A plain `git rebase <upstream>` always replays every commit on your branch that isn't in `<upstream>`.

## Syntax

```
git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> [<branch>]
```

This takes the commits in `<upstream>..<branch>` (the commits on `<branch>` that aren't in `<upstream>`) and replays them on top of `<newbase>`. If you leave out `<branch>`, it uses the current branch.

In short: **cut everything after `<upstream>` and paste it onto `<newbase>`.**

## Example: move a branch off another feature branch

You started `feature-b` from `feature-a`, but `feature-b` doesn't actually depend on it. You want it based directly on `main`:

```
Before:
main:       A---B
                 \
feature-a:        C---D
                       \
feature-b:              E---F
```

```bash
git rebase --onto main feature-a feature-b
```

Git takes the commits after `feature-a` (just `E` and `F`) and replays them onto `main`:

```
After:
main:       A---B
                |\
feature-a:      | C---D
                 \
feature-b:        E'---F'
```

A plain `git rebase main` run on `feature-b` would have carried `C` and `D` along too. `--onto` leaves them behind.

## Other common uses

- **Delete commits from the middle of a branch:** `git rebase --onto HEAD~3 HEAD~2` drops the commit `HEAD~2` and keeps the commits after it.
- **After an upstream branch was squash-merged or rewritten:** `git rebase --onto main <old-feature-a-sha>` replays only your own commits, so the old ones that are already merged don't come back.

As with any rebase, the replayed commits get new SHAs (`E'`, `F'`). If the branch was already pushed, you'll need `git push --force-with-lease`.
